content: Furazolidone is a nitrofuran-based antibacterial agent that has been marketed under various brand names, including Furoxone by Roberts Laboratories and Dependal-M, Diafuron, and Medaron by GlaxoSmithKline. Uses of Furazolidone Spectrum of Activity Furazolidone exhibits a broad spectrum of antimicrobial activity, targeting a variety of pathogens. It is effective against: Gram-positive bacteria: Clostridium perfringens Corynebacterium pyogenes Streptococci Staphylococci Gram-negative bacteria: Escherichia coli Salmonella dublin Salmonella typhimurium Protozoa: Giardia lamblia Eimeria species Histomonas meleagridis Use in Humans Furazolidone has been employed in the treatment of bacterial and protozoal infections that cause diarrhea and enteritis. It has been used to manage conditions such as traveler’s diarrhea, cholera, and bacteremic salmonellosis. Additionally, its potential use in treating Helicobacter pylori infections has been proposed. For giardiasis caused by Giardia lamblia, furazolidone is an option, though it is not considered a first-line treatment. The dosing recommendations are as follows: Adults: 100 mg taken four times daily, typically for 2–5 days. In some cases, treatment may extend up to 7 days, or up to 10 days for giardiasis. Children: 1.25 mg/kg administered four times daily, usually for 2–5 days, or up to 10 days for giardiasis. It is essential to adhere to the most recent local guidelines and recommendations when prescribing or using this medication. Use in Animals In veterinary medicine, furazolidone has been used to treat infections caused by Myxobolus cerebralis in salmonids and has also been utilized in aquaculture. However, due to its classification as a nitrofuran antibiotic, the use of furazolidone in food-producing animals is prohibited by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) under the Animal Medicinal Drug Use Clarification Act of 1994. Use in Laboratory Settings Furazolidone has been employed in laboratory settings to differentiate between micrococci and staphylococci. Mechanism of Action The antimicrobial activity of furazolidone is believed to result from its ability to crosslink DNA, thereby interfering with the replication and transcription processes of the target microorganisms. Side Effects and Safety Concerns Furazolidone is no longer available in the United States due to its side effect profile and safety concerns. While it has demonstrated efficacy against highly drug-resistant infections, its use is associated with significant systemic toxicity. Adverse effects include: Neurological symptoms such as tremors and convulsions Peripheral neuritis Gastrointestinal disturbances Depression of spermatogenesis Furthermore, nitrofurans, including furazolidone, have been identified by the FDA as mutagenic and carcinogenic agents. As a result, their use has been banned in the United States since 1991.
